entry.title: The Last Flight Out of Kham Duc — Vietnam’s Most Desperate Airlift

media:group.media:title: The Last Flight Out of Kham Duc — Vietnam’s Most Desperate Airlift
media:group.media:description:
On May 12, 1968, the U.S. command in Vietnam made a rare decision: abandon a base under attack and fly everyone out. This is the Battle of Kham Duc, and the story of the last flight out.
Kham Duc was the last Special Forces camp watching the Ho Chi Minh Trail in that part of South Vietnam. It sat in a valley ringed by hills, and by the morning of May 12 the North Vietnamese 2nd Division held those hills. Two days earlier, the nearby outpost at Ngok Tavak, held by Australian advisers, a Mike Force company and a platoon of U.S. Marine artillerymen, had been overrun in a night attack.
Now well over a thousand soldiers and civilians had to be lifted off a single runway under fire. Helicopters were hit on the strip. A C-130 carrying around 150 civilians was shot down just after takeoff. And after the evacuation was declared complete, three Air Force combat controllers were still on the ground, until Lt. Col. Joe Jackson brought his C-123 down onto the burning airstrip to get them out. He received the Medal of Honor for it.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ THE BATTLE ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 📅 Date: May 10–12, 1968 (Ngok Tavak: May 10 / Kham Duc evacuation: May 12) 📍 Location: Kham Duc Special Forces camp, Quang Tin Province, South Vietnam 🇺🇸 U.S. & allied forces: 5th Special Forces Group, CIDG and Mike Force, Australian advisers (AATTV), U.S. Marines, Americal Division (2/1st Infantry, 196th Light Infantry Brigade), U.S. Air Force airlift crews 🇻🇳 North Vietnamese forces: elements of the PAVN 2nd Division ⚔️ Losses: Disputed. Between 12 and 16 Americans were killed at Ngok Tavak alone, and 31 Americans were listed missing across both battles. Hundreds of South Vietnamese irregulars and civilians died. Estimates of North Vietnamese losses range from about 345 to several thousand. 🎖️ Awards: Medal of Honor, Lt. Col. Joe M. Jackson. Air Force Cross, Maj. Bernard Bucher (posthumous), Lt. Col. Daryl Cole and others
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ CHAPTERS ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 00:00 – The decision to abandon Kham Duc 01:30 – A camp on the edge of the Ho Chi Minh Trail 04:00 – The fall of Ngok Tavak 07:30 – Surrounded: the morning of May 12 10:00 – Evacuation under fire 13:00 – The loss of Bucher's C-130 15:00 – Three men left behind 16:30 – Joe Jackson's last flight out 18:00 – Aftermath: "Khe Sanh in reverse"
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ MYTH vs. RECORD ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ ❌ "183 people died aboard the C-130." ✅ Most reliable accounts put it at around 150 civilians plus the crew and a Special Forces officer. The higher number appears in some online sources but is not supported.
❌ "Ngok Tavak fell on May 6." ✅ Multiple sources confirm the attack began around 3:00 a.m. on May 10, 1968.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ SOURCES ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ • Air & Space Forces Magazine – "Rescue at Kham Duc" • U.S. Air Force historical accounts of the Kham Duc airlift • Vietnam Helicopter Pilots Association records • Veteran accounts from 2/1st Infantry and Kham Duc survivors • Congressional Medal of Honor Society – Joe M. entry.title: What Really Happened to the Black Lions in Vietnam? | Ong Thanh 1967

media:group.media:title: What Really Happened to the Black Lions in Vietnam? | Ong Thanh 1967
media:group.media:description:
What really happened to the Black Lions at Ong Thanh? On October 17, 1967, an American battalion went back into the jungle northwest of Saigon to find a Viet Cong regiment. Within half an hour its lead company had been destroyed. By noon its commander was dead, and around sixty Americans would never leave that jungle. Then the official version called it a victory.
This is the full story of the Battle of Ong Thanh, one of the costliest ambushes American troops suffered in Vietnam, and of the men who fought it. Lt. Col. Terry Allen Jr., son of the general who led the Big Red One in World War II. Lt. Clark Welch, who questioned the mission the night before and later refused to leave his wounded. Forward observer Lt. Harold "Pinky" Durham, who kept calling in artillery after losing a hand. And Maj. Don Holleder, the West Point football All-American who ran into the jungle to bring the wounded out.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ THE BATTLE ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Date: 17 October 1967 Location: Ong Thanh stream near Chon Thanh, about 40 miles northwest of Saigon Operation: Shenandoah II US force: 2nd Battalion, 28th Infantry "Black Lions", 1st Infantry Division. Companies A and D and the battalion command group, fewer than 150 men Enemy: Viet Cong 271st Regiment, 9th Division. Estimates range from several hundred to more than a thousand men US losses: between 57 and 64 killed depending on the source, about 75 wounded, 2 missing and never recovered Awards: Medal of Honor for 2nd Lt. Harold B. Durham Jr. Distinguished Service Cross for Lt. Col. Terry Allen Jr., 1st Lt. Clark Welch and Maj. Don Holleder
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ CHAPTERS ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 0:00 "The trees are moving" 1:48 A new strategy in Hanoi and a hungry regiment 5:09 The Black Lions and the argument the night before 8:46 Into the ambush 12:25 The cease-fire order 14:55 Durham, Allen and Holleder 18:08 Around sixty dead, and a victory announced 20:38 Thirty-five years later
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ MYTH VS. RECORD ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Myth: The Black Lions were ambushed by the North Vietnamese Army. Record: The attackers were the Viet Cong 271st Regiment, one of the most experienced Viet Cong main-force regiments in the region.
Myth: The Americans won the battle. Record: The division reported a victory and claimed 101 enemy dead. Historians consider that figure inflated, and the survivors always said they had been ambushed and beaten.
Myth: The Viet Cong regiment came to Ong Thanh looking for a fight. Record: According to David Maraniss, the 271st had stopped near the stream because it was waiting for rice that never arrived.
A note on the numbers: sources give different totals for the American dead, from 57 to 64, depending on whether men who died of wounds later and men from attached units are counted. Enemy losses are unknown. This video gives the figures as ranges rather than picking one.

entry.title: What Marines Faced in Helicopter Valley — The Most Brutal Battle of 1966

media:group.media:title: What Marines Faced in Helicopter Valley — The Most Brutal Battle of 1966
media:group.media:description:
July 18th, 1966. One company of U.S. Marines was ordered to stay behind in Helicopter Valley while the rest of the battalion pulled out. Then an estimated thousand North Vietnamese soldiers came out of the jungle.
This is Operation Hastings, the 1966 Vietnam War battle that began when an entire NVA division crossed the DMZ into Quang Tri Province. About 8,000 U.S. Marines and 3,000 South Vietnamese troops went in to stop it. What they found in the Song Ngan valley gave it a new name before the first day was over.
In this Vietnam War documentary: ▸ The prisoner and the defector who revealed a North Vietnamese division south of the DMZ ▸ The landing at LZ Crow, where three CH-46 Sea Knights were wrecked on the first morning ▸ The helicopter shot down in flames into the Marines' own command post ▸ Three nights of attacks on Company K, 3rd Battalion, 4th Marines ▸ Force Recon Marines rappelling onto the Rockpile to call in artillery ▸ The rear-guard fight at LZ Crow, and two Medals of Honor ▸ Hill 362, Typhoon Ora, and a third Medal of Honor ▸ Why Operation Hastings turned the DMZ into a front line for years
Operation Hastings cost 126 Marines killed and 448 wounded. It ended on August 3rd, 1966, and on the same day the Marines started a new operation on the same ground. Con Thien, Operation Buffalo and Khe Sanh all came after this.

entry.title: The Most Brutal Vietnam War Battles of 1968 — America’s Deadliest Year

media:group.media:title: The Most Brutal Vietnam War Battles of 1968 — America’s Deadliest Year
media:group.media:description:
Vietnam War stories from 1968, America's deadliest year of the Vietnam War. This full Vietnam War documentary covers the most brutal Vietnam War battles of 1968: the Siege of Khe Sanh, the Tet Offensive, the Battle of Hue, Operation Scotland II and the Battle of Dai Do. Vietnam War history explained through the US Marines and American soldiers who fought it.
In January 1968, Washington told the American public the Vietnam War was being won. Within weeks, US Marines were surrounded at Khe Sanh Combat Base and shelled day and night by the North Vietnamese Army (NVA). Then the Viet Cong and the NVA launched the Tet Offensive, attacking cities and bases across South Vietnam at the same time. In Hue, US Marines fought house by house in the most brutal urban combat of the Vietnam War. And long after the headlines moved on, Marines kept fighting and dying in battles almost nobody remembers.
By the end of 1968, more American soldiers had been killed in Vietnam than in any other year of the war.
🎖️ The Vietnam War battles in this documentary:
▬ Khe Sanh 1968 – The Siege of Khe Sanh: US Marines cut off near the DMZ, surrounded by NVA divisions ▬ The Tet Offensive 1968 – The surprise attack that changed the Vietnam War forever ▬ The Battle of Hue 1968 – 26 days of street fighting as US Marines retook the old imperial capital ▬ Operation Scotland II – The forgotten Marine war in the hills around Khe Sanh ▬ The Battle of Dai Do 1968 – Marines against a dug-in NVA force along the Cua Viet River
This is Vietnam War history explained battle by battle: the tactics, the decisions and the men on the ground. If you like Vietnam War documentaries, Vietnam War stories, US Marines history and real military history, this full documentary is for you.

entry.title: Green Berets Trapped in a Bunker as Enemy Tanks Rolled Overhead | Vietnam War

media:group.media:title: Green Berets Trapped in a Bunker as Enemy Tanks Rolled Overhead | Vietnam War
media:group.media:description:
In February 1968, a small team of U.S. Army Green Berets was trapped inside a concrete bunker at Lang Vei Special Forces Camp while North Vietnamese tanks rolled over their positions, and one even climbed onto the bunker itself. The Marine base at Khe Sanh was only miles away. Help never came.
This Vietnam War documentary tells the full story of the Battle of Lang Vei, the night North Vietnam launched its first major tank assault inside South Vietnam. Detachment A-101 of the 5th Special Forces Group, together with Montagnard and South Vietnamese fighters, faced Soviet-built PT-76 tanks, sappers, flamethrowers and an entire NVA regiment, armed mostly with M72 LAW rockets that often failed to explode.
You’ll see how the warnings were missed, why the Marines at Khe Sanh refused to send a relief force, how the defenders survived hours of explosives and tear gas inside the bunker, and how Sergeant First Class Eugene Ashley Jr. led five counterattacks to break them out, earning a posthumous Medal of Honor.

entry.title: Operation Dewey Canyon: The Marines’ Secret Raid Into Laos (1969)

media:group.media:title: Operation Dewey Canyon: The Marines’ Secret Raid Into Laos (1969)
media:group.media:description:
In February 1969, U.S. Marines crossed into Laos and ambushed North Vietnamese trucks on the Ho Chi Minh Trail, in a country where American ground troops were officially not fighting. This is Operation Dewey Canyon, one of the last major Marine offensives of the Vietnam War.
For 56 days, Col. Robert Barrow's 9th Marines fought their way through the Da Krong and A Shau valleys toward Base Area 611, a North Vietnamese supply hub on the Laotian border. They battled fog that grounded every helicopter, 122mm guns firing from across the border, and a night sapper attack on Fire Support Base Cunningham. Then, on the night of February 21–22, two platoons of Hotel Company, 2nd Battalion, 9th Marines, slipped onto Route 922 in Laos and destroyed three trucks. Days later, three Marine companies marched down the Trail itself.
Four Marines received the Medal of Honor: Thomas Noonan, Wesley Fox, William Morgan and Alfred Wilson. The Marines captured about 500 tons of weapons and ammunition, one of the largest hauls of the war. And the Marines who died in Laos were officially recorded as killed in South Vietnam.

entry.title: Surrounded in Grenada: The SEALS Who Called for Help on the Governor’s Phone

media:group.media:title: Surrounded in Grenada: The SEALS Who Called for Help on the Governor’s Phone
media:group.media:description:
The Grenada Invasion of 1983, Operation Urgent Fury, is remembered as a quick American victory. But for SEAL Team 6, Delta Force and the Night Stalkers, the US invasion of Grenada was the day almost everything went wrong. This Grenada documentary tells the full story.
In October 1983, a bloody coup killed Grenada’s prime minister, Maurice Bishop. With nearly 600 American medical students on the island and Cuban influence growing, President Ronald Reagan ordered the invasion of Grenada. It was one of the first American combat operations since Vietnam and a major Cold War flashpoint in the Caribbean.
Before the Grenada invasion even began, four Navy SEALs from SEAL Team 6 were lost at sea. Over Richmond Hill Prison, Delta Force and Army Rangers ran into hidden anti-aircraft guns, and a Black Hawk pilot from the 160th Night Stalkers was killed. At the governor’s mansion, 22 Navy SEALs lost their commander and their satellite radio, then held out against Grenadian troops and Soviet-built BTR-60 armored cars. At the radio station, another SEAL team escaped into the sea. Marine Cobra pilots died over St. George’s, and AC-130 Spectre gunships fought through the night to keep the SEALs alive.
When their radios died, the SEALs called for help on the governor’s own telephone. This is the true story behind the famous Grenada “payphone” legend, and of how the failures of Operation Urgent Fury helped create U.S. Special Operations Command (SOCOM).

entry.title: Before the Siege: The First Battle of Khe Sanh (1967)

media:group.media:title: Before the Siege: The First Battle of Khe Sanh (1967)
media:group.media:description:
Nine months before the siege of Khe Sanh, U.S. Marines fought a brutal, almost forgotten battle for the very same hills. This is the First Battle of Khe Sanh, the Hill Fights of 1967.
On April 24th, 1967, a five-man Marine team climbing Hill 861 walked into the North Vietnamese 325C Division, dug in around the Marine base at Khe Sanh. What followed was nearly three weeks of fighting for Hill 861, Hill 881 South and Hill 881 North. Platoons were cut down in front of hidden bunkers. Wounded Marines were carried off the hills through fog and rain. A company went up Hill 881 South with 161 men and lost more than half of them killed or wounded. And many Marines fought with a brand-new M16 rifle that kept jamming, a problem that would end up in front of the U.S. Congress.
Roughly 160 Marines were killed taking three hills. Nine months later, the North Vietnamese came back, and the siege of Khe Sanh began.

entry.title: The Soldier Who Sang Under Fire — And Saved 2,700 Lives on 9/11

media:group.media:title: The Soldier Who Sang Under Fire — And Saved 2,700 Lives on 9/11
media:group.media:description:
He survived the Battle of Ia Drang. 36 years later, he saved 2,700 lives on 9/11. This is the true story of Rick Rescorla and the 7th Cavalry Regiment, America’s most battle-hardened unit of the Vietnam War.
In November 1965, the 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile) fought the first major battle between the U.S. Army and the North Vietnamese Army in the Ia Drang Valley. At LZ X-Ray, Lt. Col. Hal Moore’s men were surrounded and outnumbered. Days later at LZ Albany, the 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry walked into one of the deadliest ambushes of the entire Vietnam War. Among them was a young British-born platoon leader who sang to keep his men calm under fire: Rick Rescorla.
In this Vietnam War documentary we follow the 7th Cavalry through six years of relentless combat: ✅ The Battle of Ia Drang: LZ X-Ray and LZ Albany (1965) ✅ Operation Pershing, the longest operation in 1st Cavalry Division history ✅ The Tet Offensive and the Battle of Hue (1968) ✅ Operation Pegasus and the relief of Khe Sanh ✅ Rick Rescorla’s journey from Vietnam War hero to head of security at Morgan Stanley in the World Trade Center
Rescorla was the soldier featured in “We Were Soldiers Once… and Young.” On September 11, 2001, he evacuated thousands of people from the South Tower, then went back inside. He was never seen again.
One soldier. Two wars. One extraordinary life.

entry.title: The SAS in WW2: Executed Under Hitler's Commando Order

media:group.media:title: The SAS in WW2: Executed Under Hitler's Commando Order
media:group.media:description:
WW2 SAS documentary: the true story of Operation Bulbasket and Hitler's Commando Order. 40 SAS soldiers dropped into occupied France in 1944 — betrayed, and 34 executed.
In June 1944, forty men of B Squadron, 1st Special Air Service, parachuted into occupied France with one job: cut the railway lines feeding German reinforcements to Normandy. They succeeded. They helped bring about the destruction of a German fuel train headed for the 2nd SS Panzer Division, Das Reich.
Then their forest camp near Verrières was betrayed. Captured soldiers, an American pilot who had joined them, and seven French Resistance fighters were executed, in line with Hitler's Commando Order of 1942, which condemned captured Allied special forces to death.
This WW2 documentary follows Operation Bulbasket from the night drop into France to the postwar investigation into what happened at Verrières and St Sauvant.

entry.title: Why Nobody Remembers New Zealand Fought in Vietnam

media:group.media:title: Why Nobody Remembers New Zealand Fought in Vietnam
media:group.media:description:
In August 1966, three New Zealand gunners called in artillery through a monsoon at the Battle of Long Tan, and helped save D Company from being overrun. Almost nobody remembers they were there.
This is the forgotten story of New Zealand in the Vietnam War. Close to 3,500 New Zealanders served between 1963 and 1972, and 37 never came home. Yet because their units were folded into Australian formations, their battles are almost always remembered as purely Australian.
In this documentary, we follow New Zealand's war from the first civilian surgical team in 1963 to the final withdrawal in 1971:
▸ 161 Battery, Royal New Zealand Artillery, and the forward observer team of Captain Maurice Stanley, Lance-Bombardier Murray Broomhall and Signaller Willie Walker at Long Tan ▸ Victor Company and Whisky Company, the Kiwi riflemen of the ANZAC battalions at Nui Dat ▸ The New Zealand SAS troop running long-range reconnaissance in Phuoc Tuy province ▸ The Battle of Nui Le in 1971, the last major battle Australia and New Zealand fought together in Vietnam ▸ The homecoming nobody gave them, and the official welcome that only came in 2008
Which allied force from the Vietnam War deserves its own deep dive next? Tell us in the comments.

entry.title: The Forgotten Siege Before Ia Drang That Nobody Talks About

media:group.media:title: The Forgotten Siege Before Ia Drang That Nobody Talks About
media:group.media:description:
In the summer of 1965, a tiny Green Beret camp on the Cambodian border was surrounded by a North Vietnamese regiment — and every helicopter unit in the region refused to fly in. This is the forgotten Battle of Duc Co, the siege that gave Norman Schwarzkopf his first taste of combat, and the rehearsal for the Battle of the Ia Drang Valley.
For more than two months, a handful of US Special Forces soldiers and their Montagnard fighters held out at Duc Co in Vietnam's Central Highlands. The camp was never the real target. It was bait. North Vietnamese General Chu Huy Man wanted to draw a relief column down Highway 19 — the same road where the French Groupe Mobile 100 was destroyed in 1954 — and ambush it on ground he had already chosen.
When a force of South Vietnamese paratroopers, with a young Major Schwarzkopf as their adviser, walked straight into that trap, the rescuers suddenly needed rescuing themselves. Inside the camp, ammunition was nearly gone. Then two Air Commando pilots overheard the words "suicide mission" and volunteered to fly a C-123 into Duc Co anyway.
In this documentary you'll discover: ▸ Why the Special Forces border camps were so vulnerable in 1965 ▸ Who the Montagnards were — the forgotten allies of the Vietnam War ▸ The North Vietnamese plan to cut South Vietnam in two ▸ The C-123 resupply flight under heavy machine gun fire ▸ Major Colt Terry's charge down the runway — and the Silver Star he never received ▸ Schwarzkopf's infamous encounter with General Westmoreland ▸ How Duc Co became the blueprint for Plei Me and the Ia Drang
Most people know the Ia Drang from "We Were Soldiers." Almost nobody knows that the same tactic was tested three months earlier at Duc Co.

entry.title: The Vietnam Operation 10 Times Bigger Than My Lai — And Nobody Knows It

media:group.media:title: The Vietnam Operation 10 Times Bigger Than My Lai — And Nobody Knows It
media:group.media:description:
Between December 1968 and May 1969, one U.S. Army division reported 10,889 enemy casualties in Vietnam's Mekong Delta. It recovered only 748 weapons. Those two numbers cannot both be true.
This is Operation Speedy Express — the Vietnam War operation the U.S. Army investigated, confirmed, and then locked in a filing cabinet for thirty years.
Everyone knows My Lai. Almost nobody knows this.
In this Vietnam War documentary we follow the 9th Infantry Division through six months in the Mekong Delta under Major General Julian Ewell, the commander his own soldiers called the Butcher of the Delta. We look at the free-fire zones, the body-count system that drove the fighting, and the kill ratio of 134 to 1 that no unit in American history had ever produced.
We cover:
- Why the Viet Cong controlled the Mekong Delta, and why that made every village a target - How free-fire zones redefined what counted as an enemy - The letter a sergeant wrote to General Westmoreland describing a My Lai every month - The Ben Tre hospital records: 1,431 of 1,882 injured civilians hit by American firepower - The Army Inspector General finding of 5,000 to 7,000 civilian casualties - Why no officer and no soldier was ever charged - The handbook Ewell published in 1974 teaching other commanders his methods
If you watch Vietnam War documentaries and military history, this is the operation missing from almost every one of them.
